extracted.intended_audience: politically engaged British public / readers interested in constitutional theory and parliamentary reform
extracted.subtask_description: Normative principles and warnings about how the House of Commons ought to function in a constitutional monarchy — its proper character, checks on executive power, electoral integrity, and financial/accounting practice. The text articulates standards for what constitutes a healthy vs. corrupted Commons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commons as the express image of the nation's feelings
rubrics_metrics.description: The virtue, spirit, and essence of a House of Commons consists in its being the express image of the feelings of the nation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The House should bear a stamp of the actual disposition of the people at large; it was not intended as part of the standing government but as a control issuing immediately from the people (analogous to juries). If the Commons become wholly untouched by public opinion, 'they would cease to be a House of Commons.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Commons must be a control for the people, not upon them
rubrics_metrics.description: The House of Commons was designed as a control for the people, not as an instrument to act upon or suppress the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Its true characteristics include a vigilant and jealous eye over executory and judicial magistracy, an anxious care of public money, and openness to public complaint. It was never intended as an institution for supporting peace and subordination as a primary function (it has no enforcement power beyond mace and serjeant-at-arms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commons must remain responsive to constituents (frequent elections)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever accommodations time requires, the Commons' character cannot be sustained unless it bears some stamp of the actual disposition of the people; frequent recourse to the legislature and regular elections are necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parliaments should sit frequently (the text argues for annual sittings though acknowledging practical adjustments like septennial parliaments); the habit of prolonged authority and infrequent elections pushes the Commons towards a standing senate and weakens its representative character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid indiscriminate support of ministers (sign of corruption)
rubrics_metrics.description: A symptom of total corruption is a rule of indiscriminate support to all ministers, because this destroys Parliament's end as a control and becomes a prior sanction to misgovernment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parliament should not adopt a blanket policy of supporting ministers irrespective of merit; such a disposition nullifies the corrective purpose of the Commons and facilitates arbitrary government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect the right of free election (oppose claims adverse to it)
rubrics_metrics.description: Another symptom of corruption is setting up claims adverse to the right of free election; such claims subvert the legal authority by which the House sits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any attempt to alter or undermine the right of election (for example by making the Commons able to disable members at pleasure) tends to convert representation into a fiction and to displace popular authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliament must not assume executive functions or act as a court of criminal equity
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislative bodies should not adopt discretionary criminal jurisdictions (a 'criminal equity') or perform the offices of executive government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carrying offences into legislative bodies, or permitting discretionary punishment unbounded by law and legal evidence, revives the evils of the Star Chamber; whether it be a committee, Commons, or Lords, such jurisdiction subverts the liberty of the subject and destroys the proper end of the House.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve impeachment as guardian of the constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: Impeachment is a great guardian of the purity of the constitution and must be preserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If Parliament participates in executive acts (or the whole executive is done 'in Parliament'), the Commons loses proper ground to punish or impeach others for acts in which it has been complicit; preserving impeachment requires separation of functions and accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: The right of election must be bonâ fide, not a legal fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: The right of election is meant to give the people 'that man, and that man only, whom ... they declare that they know, esteem, love, and trust.' It is not merely a formal matter satisfiable by substitutes or legal fictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substituting fictitious persons or legal constructs (the Titius/Mævius, John Doe/Richard Roe analogies) defeats the end of representation. Representation is a matter of actual choice and feeling, not technical formalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Commons must not have arbitrary discretionary power to declare incapacities
rubrics_metrics.description: It is improper for the House to claim a power of discretionary disqualification without any rule, principle, or fixed standard for declaring unfitness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The House's asserted power to declare incapacities based only on its 'discretion' (with no specification of the principle, degree, mode of proceeding, or evidence) would forfeit the franchise for offences unknown and unprovable by legal rules — an anomaly to the constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgment must not be made the source of law (no law by occasional will)
rubrics_metrics.description: A tribunal that 'declares' law by its occasional will, when its judgment becomes law without appeal or rule, usurps legislative power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a body asserts that 'what we declare to be law becomes law' independent of legal principle or appeal, legality follows arbitrary discretion; this is the nature of a legislative act masquerading as adjudication and is incompatible with constitutional safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public accounts should be presented and examined before payment
rubrics_metrics.description: The capital use of an account is that the reality, reason, and justice of the charge should appear antecedent to the payment; an account after payment is of no rational purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Previous production of every account is a key check on corrupt and prodigal use of public money. Paying first and taking accounts later establishes the dangerous precedent of 'payment previous to account' and undermines parliamentary stewardship of the public purse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid making the Commons financially dependent on the crown
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'unlimited fund of money' laid out according to the pleasure of the court would secure the Commons against deviation towards popularity and make it dependent on the crown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Destroying appropriations and revenue limits converts the Commons into an instrument of the court; fiscal independence and restrictions on appropriations are essential to preserve representative independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust the people with their privileges rather than concentrating franchise control in Commons
rubrics_metrics.description: The people are best trusted to exercise their own privileges; they do not desire the House's intervention to free them from the burden of privilege.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The constitution reposed no such confidence in the Commons as to give them power over franchises; giving a body uncontrolled discretionary power over people's rights invites abuse and is contrary to the spirit of the law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid institutional incentives that discourage independent members
rubrics_metrics.description: A system where court-connected members reap honors, offices, emoluments and patronage while independent representatives are excluded creates circumstances that discourage faithful service by independent members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If popularity exposes a man to disqualification while servility preserves and rewards him, the principles of popular election and honest representation are perverted; the Commons cannot be a genuine control unless members are protected by constituents and not bought or starved out by patronage.
